Getting started with stabl

Source: vignettes/stablr-getting-started.Rmd
stablr-getting-started.Rmd

1 Introduction

stabl() is the high-level entry point to stablr. Given a table of features and an outcome, it runs STABL with statistically safe defaults and returns an object that states, in plain language, which features were selected and how reliable the selection is estimated to be.

The full contract is as follows.

fit <- stabl(my_data, y = "response")
fit

Everything else in the package is available when more control is required; see Section 5, The expert interface.

2 A worked example

The example uses a small simulated proteomic-style dataset: 60 samples and 8 features, of which two truly drive the outcome.

set.seed(1L)
df <- data.frame(
  m1 = rnorm(60), m2 = rnorm(60), m3 = rnorm(60), m4 = rnorm(60),
  m5 = rnorm(60), n1 = rnorm(60), n2 = rnorm(60), n3 = rnorm(60)
)
df$response <- 0.9 * df$m1 + 0.9 * df$m2 + rnorm(60, sd = 0.4)

STABL is fitted with a reduced number of bootstraps so that the vignette knits quickly; the default (n_bootstraps = 1000) should be used in practice.

library(stablr)
fit <- stabl(df, y = "response", n_bootstraps = 200L, random_state = 1L)

Printing the fit gives the plain-language answer.

fit
#> <stabl stability selection>
#>   outcome family: gaussian | base learner: lasso | bootstraps: 200
#>   3 feature(s) selected at FDP+ estimate 0.333:
#>   m1, m2, n3
#>   use summary() for details, plot() for stability paths,
#>   get_feature_names() / get_support() for the selection,
#>   get_fdrs() for the FDP+ curve.

The printed output reports the selected features together with the estimated reliability of the selection.

The selected features are also available as a character vector.

get_feature_names(fit)
#> [1] "m1" "m2" "n3"

summary() adds the stability threshold and the FDP+ estimate.

summary(fit)
#> <stabl stability selection summary>
#>   features considered : 8
#>   bootstraps          : 200
#>   stability threshold : 0.990
#>   FDP+ estimate       : 0.333
#>   selected (3)       : m1, m2, n3

The plot() method draws the stability paths and the FDP+ curve.

plot(fit)

The figure shows the stability paths of the features across the lambda grid together with the FDP+ curve used for calibration.

3 Defaults chosen by stabl()

Decision Default chosen Why
Artificial features model-X knockoffs (knockoff_equi) conservative decoys for tree learners; measured calibration is learner- and regime-dependent — see the pairing table in vignette("stablr-intro") before trusting FDP+
Calibration FDP+ on (no fixed hard_threshold) the threshold is chosen to control the estimated false discovery proportion rather than fixed by hand
Knockoff failure knockoff_fallback = "stop" a silent fallback would silently change what the FDP+ estimates mean
Lambda grid automatic a sensible grid is derived from the data

Any expert argument — artificial_proportion, sample_fraction, sample_groups, a custom adapter — is passed through ....

fit <- stabl(df, y = "response", base_learner = "elastic_net",
             artificial_proportion = 0.5)

4 Leakage-safe preprocessing

The worked example above fits on the full dataset. That is correct for exploratory selection — the selection describes the data you have. The moment you want held-out predictions or a train/test evaluation, one rule applies to every learned transform (centering, scaling, imputation, variance filtering):

Fit the transform on the training samples only; apply the stored training parameters to the test samples.

Two shortcuts both corrupt the analysis. Fitting the transform on the pooled train + test data leaks test-distribution information into training — the test means and variances shift the fitted parameters, and the held-out estimate is optimistically biased. Fitting a separate transform on the test data is not leakage, but it places the test samples in a different feature space, so a model trained on the training transform mispredicts them.

stabl_preprocess_fit() and stabl_preprocess_apply() implement the rule as a fit/apply pair.

x <- as.matrix(df[, 1:8])
idx <- seq_len(40)  # first 40 samples train, remaining 20 test

pp <- stabl_preprocess_fit(x[idx, ], transforms = c("center", "scale"))
x_train <- stabl_preprocess_apply(pp, x[idx, ])
x_test  <- stabl_preprocess_apply(pp, x[-idx, ])

pp stores the training means and standard deviations, and x_test is scaled with those values — not with its own. You can see the difference: the test matrix is centred with the training means, so its own column means are not exactly zero.

round(colMeans(x_test), 3)
#>     m1     m2     m3     m4     m5     n1     n2     n3 
#>  0.053  0.003  0.830 -0.396  0.087 -0.142  0.182  0.588

The same rule is applied automatically inside every fold of stabl_analyze(mode = "validated") and inside the multi-omic cross-validation workflows, so a validated analysis cannot leak through preprocessing. For the multi-view case — including why the validation matrix must be transformed with the training parameters before late-fusion prediction — see vignette("stablr-multiomic").

5 The expert interface

stabl() is a thin wrapper around stabl_fit(), the expert interface with full control over all arguments (lambda grids, bootstrap design, thresholds, learner adapters, grouping). Every stabl() result is also a valid stabl_fit object, so the entire expert toolkit applies unchanged.

# accessors (identical on stabl and stabl_fit objects)
head(get_stabl_scores(fit))

# the multiomic workflows, metrics, and plotting helpers all accept
# stabl_fit objects — including the one you just built with stabl()
class(fit)
#> [1] "stabl"     "stabl_fit"

The printed accessors show the stability scores, the FDP+ summary, and the class of the fitted object, which confirms that a stabl() result can be treated as a stabl_fit object. Read ?stabl_fit for the full expert interface, and the other vignettes for multi-omic workflows, nested cross-validation, and environment stability. For single-cell-derived feature matrices, the Single-cell integrations articles show the same workflow on cEBMF-denoised expression (vignette("stablr-cebmf")) and on metacell-pooled expression (vignette("stablr-metacells")). For what “Python parity” does and does not establish, see vignette("stablr-python-parity"); for a guide to the stability-path and FDP+ diagnostic plots, see vignette("stablr-reading-plots").

6 Migrating from pre-1.0.0 versions

The 1.0.0 contract removes the pre-0.3.0 compatibility names outright (get_feature_names_out(), stacked_multi_omic(), jaccard_matrix(), adjusted_similarity_values(), adjusted_similarity_measure(), pearson_similarity_values(), pearson_similarity_measure(), classic_bootstrap_indices()); calling them now raises an error. Use the canonical names — get_feature_names(), stabl_multiomic_stacked(), jaccard_similarity_matrix(), adjusted_similarity_pairwise(), adjusted_similarity_summary(), pearson_similarity_pairwise(), pearson_similarity_summary() — and see NEWS.md and docs/MIGRATION_0.3_TO_1.0.md for the full mapping. Bootstrap index generation (the classic_bootstrap_indices() replacement) is internal machinery; control resampling through stabl_fit()’s n_bootstraps, stratify_bootstrap, bootstrap_strata, and sample_groups arguments.

The 1.0.0 contract also removes a small set of legacy behaviors (Phase 13 PR-A): the explore/n_explore arguments of stabl_fit() (an empty selection now stays empty instead of being relabelled as a top-N “explore” set), the in-sample late_fusion_training = "python_legacy" mode, and cooperation_selection = "validation" (both biased performance estimates). The beginner generics support() and feature_names() are removed in favour of the canonical accessors get_support() and get_feature_names(), and the experimental oblique random-forest learner (base_learner = "oblique_rf") is retired (use "rf"); see the migration guide for the complete list.
